{{Short description|English physicist (1922–2004)}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=November 2019}}
'''Sir Alan Hugh Cook''' [[Fellow of the Royal Society|FRS]]<ref name="frs">{{Cite journal | last1 = Quinn | first1 = T. | doi = 10.1098/rsbm.2005.0006 | title = Sir Alan Hugh Cook. 2 December 1922: Elected FRS 1969 | journal = [[Biographical Memoirs of Fellows of the Royal Society]] | volume = 51 | pages = 87 | year = 2005 | doi-access = free }}</ref> (2 December 1922 – 23 July 2004) was an English [[physicist]] who specialised in [[geophysics]] and [[metrology]]. He worked at the [[University of Cambridge]], [[National Physical Laboratory (UK)|National Physical Laboratory]], and the [[University of Edinburgh]]. From 1977-79 Cook was [[President of the Royal Astronomical Society]].

==Early life and education==
Cook was born in [[Felsted]], Essex in 1922. He was the eldest of the six children of Reginald Thomas Cook, a [[Her Majesty's Customs and Excise|customs and excise]] officer, and his wife, Ethel, {{nee}} Saxon. His family were active in the [[Congregational church]]; Cook became a lifelong Christian.{{cn|date=September 2024}}

He was initially educated at the village school at Felsted, then at West Leigh School in [[Leigh-on-Sea]]. From 1933 he attended at [[Westcliff High School for Boys]], a [[grammar school]] in [[Westcliff-on-Sea]]. In 1939 he won a scholarship to attend university at [[Corpus Christi College, Cambridge]], beginning in 1940.<ref name=ODNB>Malcolm S. Longair, [http://www.oxforddnb.com/view/article/93881 Cook, Sir Alan Hugh (1922–2004)’], Oxford Dictionary of National Biography, Oxford University Press, Jan 2008; online edn, Oct 2008 accessed 25 Nov 2010{{Subscription required}}</ref> As an [[undergraduate]], he studied the [[natural sciences tripos]], selecting courses in [[physical sciences]], [[biological sciences]], the [[history and philosophy of science]] and [[geology]]. He received his [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree in 1943.{{cn|date=September 2024}}

Cook graduated during [[World War Two]], so [[Conscription in the United Kingdom#Second World War|was conscripted]] into military service. He was assigned to the Admiralty Signals Establishment (now part of the [[Admiralty Research Establishment]]) as a temporary experimental officer, in the field of [[electronic counter-measures]].<ref name=ODNB/> After the war he returned to Cambridge to study for a [[doctor of philosophy]] (PhD) degree under the [[PhD supervisor|supervision]] of [[Edward Bullard]] and B. C. Browne. His [[PhD thesis]] was on precise measurements of gravity in the British Isles.{{cn|date=September 2024}}

==Academic and scientific career==
Cook developed research interests in precision measurement across the physical sciences. He performed [[post-doctoral]] research at Cambridge in [[geodesy]] and [[geophysics]].<ref name=timesobit>[http://www.timesonline.co.uk/tol/comment/obituaries/article466047.ece Sir Alan Cook]{{Dead link|date=December 2025 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}, obituary, ''[[The Times]]'', 6 August 2004{{dead link|date=September 2024}}</ref>

When Bullard moved to the [[National Physical Laboratory (United Kingdom)|National Physical Laboratory]] (NPL) at [[Teddington]], Cook moved with him,<ref name=ODNB/> joining the [[meteorology|meteorological]] department of NPL.<ref name=timesobit/> Cook performed experiments including: determining the precise density of mercury, required for atmospheric pressure measurements (see [[mmHg]]); measuring the absolute acceleration of falling bodies ([[gravimetry]]); and determining the Earth's gravitational potential, by using the precisely known orbits of the Sputnik satellites ([[satellite geodesy]]). He also contributed to precision measurements of time and length standards, particularly using hyperfine lines in the spectrum of cadmium and interference [[spectroscopy]], laser [[interferometry]] and [[maser]]s. In 1966 he became superintendent of NPL's [[quantum metrology]] division.<ref name=ODNB/>

In 1969, he was appointed [[professor]] of [[geophysics]] at [[Edinburgh University]], where he founded the geophysics department. Three years later, he became [[Jacksonian Professor of Natural Philosophy]] at the [[Cavendish Laboratory]], [[University of Cambridge]], where he set up the [[laboratory astrophysics]] group. There he performed experiments in [[microwave spectroscopy]] and tests of [[Newton's law of gravitation]] at short distances. In 1979 he became head of the Cavendish Laboratory, and from 1983 to 1993 was [[master (college)|master]] of the university's [[Selwyn College, Cambridge|Selwyn College]]. His PhD students included the future astronaut [[Michael Foale]].<ref>{{cite thesis|doi=10.17863/CAM.695|title=The far-ultraviolet spectroscopy of molecules of astrophysical interest|type=PhD|publisher=University of Cambridge|year=1982|last=Foale|first=Colin Michael}}</ref>

After retiring in 1990, he took a strong interest in the [[history of science]]. From 1996, he was the editor of ''Notes and Records of the [[Royal Society]] of London'', a history of science [[academic journal]].<ref name=ODNB/>

==Personal life==
On 30 January 1948 he married Isabell Weir Adamson. The couple had a son and a daughter. He died from cancer on 23 July 2004 at Arthur Rank House, Cambridge.<ref name=ODNB/>

==Honours and awards==
*1969: Fellow of the [[Royal Society]].<ref name="frs"/><ref name=ODNB/>
*1977-79: [[President of the Royal Astronomical Society]].{{cn|date=September 2024}}
*1988: Knighthood<ref name=ODNB/>
*1993: [[The Chree Medal and Prize]]<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.iop.org/about/awards/subject/appleton/medallists/page_38521.html |title=Appleton medal recipients |website=www.iop.org |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110309171242/http://www.iop.org/about/awards/subject/appleton/medallists/page_38521.html |archive-date=2011-03-09}} </ref>

==Publications==
* ''Gravity and the earth'' (1969)
* ''Celestial Masers'' (1977)
* ''Gravitational experiments in the laboratory'' (1993)
* ''[http://assets.cambridge.org/97805214/55978/excerpt/9780521455978_excerpt.pdf The observational foundations of physics]'' (1994)
* ''Edmond Halley: charting the heavens and the seas'' (1998)
